claim: Mid-fourteenth-century London peace ordinances survive in Liber Albus; the selected writ is dated12June regnal year37 of EdwardIII, while Alsford labels the text c.1364.
locator: Riley pp.334–336; Alsford metadata and discussion.
limit: Use c.1364 as scenario, not a claim of first enactment or a single timeless medieval code.

claim: The ordinance prohibits going armed/carrying arms in city or suburbs by day/night, with specified service-related exceptions and confiscation.
locator: p.335, That no one go armed.
limit: No claim every form of working knife was always prosecuted identically; focus on obvious sword/weapon carrying, no knight exemption.

claim: Exceptions include great lords' attendants carrying their masters' swords in their presence, royal serjeants-at-arms, city officers and those accompanying them at their command.
limit: Do not turn rich clothing, a title or carrying somebody else's sword alone into permission.

claim: Hosts must warn guests to leave arms at lodgings; if a guest carries arms because the host failed to warn, the host faces imprisonment and a discretionary fine.
limit: No fixed host fine; do not say every guest offence automatically punishes host.

claim: Drawing sword/knife/weapon without striking carries half a mark (6s8d) or15days at Newgate; shedding blood with the weapon carries20s or40days.
limit: OR, not both automatically. Selected ordinance, not all medieval courts or complete sentence outcomes.

claim: A fist blow without blood carries3s or8days; with blood40d (3s4d) or12days; good-behaviour sureties required before release.
limit: Keep p.408's2s variant out of selected code. No gore or claim victim compensated by the city's fine.

claim: Victim retains legal recovery in addition to city penalties; the text orders bloodshed cases heard before sheriffs without specified procedural delays.
limit: Only separate recovery is narrated; no claim swift trial always occurred.

claim: Curfew is rung at Our Lady/St Mary-le-Bow between day and night; wandering contrary to ordinance risks Newgate until fine and good-behaviour surety.
limit: No universal fixed hour, no curfew fine amount supplied, and no assertion all night travel forbidden.

claim: Curfew exception names a known reputable man or his servant, for good cause, with a light.
limit: Requirements work together. A lantern alone is not a permit; text's social category is not a modern ID system.

claim: Aldermen must arrange proper ward watches and maintain names of inhabitants/lodgers/workers; ward responsibility for watch failure is stated.
limit: Prescribed organization, not complete surviving roster, surveillance performance or exact watch size.

claim: Reputable men of standing may arrest felons/misdoers when officers are absent and bring them to sheriffs' houses.
limit: No general license for anyone to attack strangers; no modern police equivalence.

claim: On6March1365 William Moot, John de Henham and Thomas Fraunceys faced combined night-affray, open-door-after-curfew and nightwalking charges; committed then released same day on mainprise to keep peace.
locator: Roll A10, entry under6March1365, following Curteys detinue case.
limit: Present as charges and recorded disposition. No invented dialogue, verdict, fine or blows; label date jump.

claim: Rules and actual case records are different evidence; reputation, purpose, light and people willing to answer for behaviour matter to this system.
limit: Social interpretation bounded to sources, not certainty about every encounter or a ranking against modern policing.
